requirements/glasses-and-head-covering-r.content:
Passport photo rejections are more common than most people expect, and glasses and head coverings are two of the leading causes. Understanding the glasses and head covering rules for passport photos is not just about memorizing a list — it is about knowing why these rules exist and how to apply them before you submit your application. This guide covers every relevant scenario: prescription eyewear, cosmetic lenses, medical exemptions, regular and religious coverings across four major passport-issuing countries.

Why These Rules Exist: The ICAO Biometric Requirements

Modern passports are not just travel documents. They are biometric identity instruments. Every photo submitted to a passport authority is processed against the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Document 9303 standard — the international technical specification that governs machine-readable travel documents.

At the core of this standard is automated facial recognition. Biometric systems map specific landmarks on the human face: the distance between the pupils, the curve of the brow ridge, the geometry of the nose and jawline, and the depth of the eye sockets. Any object that partially obscures, distorts, or casts shadows over these landmarks reduces the system's ability to produce a reliable biometric template.

Glasses are a particular problem. Lens glare, frame shadows, refraction distortion through curved lenses, and frame edges that clip into the eye socket region all degrade landmark detection accuracy. Head coverings — when they cast shadows across the forehead or cheekbones, or create asymmetry in the face outline — produce similar interference.

This is why these rules are not arbitrary. They are engineering requirements baked into the identity verification infrastructure used at every border crossing, e-gate, and immigration checkpoint. See our detailed guide for biometric photos.

Glasses in Passport Photos: Country-by-Country Rules

The policies governing eyewear have diverged significantly across English-speaking countries over the past decade. Canada remains the most permissive. The USA, UK, and Australia have each moved to near-total bans, with narrow medical exceptions.

Country

Glasses Allowed?

Medical Exemption

Required Documentation

USA

No (banned since Nov 2016)

Yes

Signed statement from licensed physician

UK

No

Yes

Signed medical statement from doctor or optometrist

Canada

Yes, with conditions

N/A (generally permitted)

None required if lenses are clear and glare-free

Australia

No (banned since July 2018)

Yes

Signed medical certificate; may require B11 Form

USA — Strict Ban Since 2016

The U.S. Department of State implemented a complete ban on eyeglasses in passport photos in November 2016. The policy applies to all applicants regardless of age or vision status. Prescription glasses, reading glasses, fashion frames worn without lenses, and anti-reflective glasses are all prohibited. The only exception is a documented medical condition that makes removal physically impossible — not merely uncomfortable or inconvenient. If you qualify, your physician must provide a signed statement on letterhead confirming the medical necessity. Even with an exemption, the photo must show no glare, no shadows from frames, and fully unobstructed eyes.

Review the full US passport photo requirement list before submitting your application.

UK — No Glasses Without Medical Need

The UK government's official guidance on GOV.UK states that glasses must not appear in passport photos. The reasoning mirrors the biometric argument: lenses can create glare or reflections, cast shadows across the face, and cause distortions that interfere with automated processing. Even optically clear lenses with anti-reflective coating are prohibited under standard rules. A medical exemption is possible, requiring a signed statement from a doctor or optometrist. If granted, the photo must still meet all other requirements: no glare, no shadows, eyes fully open and visible, frames not clipping into the eye area.

Canada — Glasses Allowed With Conditions

Canada stands apart from the other three countries. Canada.ca permits prescription eyeglasses in passport photos, provided the eyes are clearly visible, there is no reflection or glare on the lenses, and the glasses are not tinted. Sunglasses are not acceptable under any circumstances. Since May 2015, tinted eyeglasses — including lightly tinted prescription lenses — have been explicitly disqualified. If your glasses create any visible glare in the photo, the application will be rejected even though glasses are technically permitted.

Australia — Similar to the USA

The Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) banned glasses from passport photos starting July 1, 2018. The rule applies to all standard applicants. A medical exemption exists for conditions such as recent eye surgery or a permanent inability to remove eyewear, but the applicant must submit a signed medical certificate alongside the application. In some cases, a B11 Form (Medical Certificate for Passport Photo) is required. Even under a medical exemption, lenses must be untinted, frames must not obscure the eyes, and no reflections are permitted in the image.

Medical Exemptions for Glasses

A medical exemption for glasses is granted in narrow circumstances. Vision impairment alone — meaning you need glasses to see — does not qualify in the USA, UK, or Australia. The exemption is reserved for situations where removal of the glasses is physically impossible due to a medical condition: for example, post-surgical fixation, severe photophobia requiring tinted lenses for medical protection, or a structural condition where the glasses cannot be safely removed.

To apply for an exemption:

  1. Obtain a signed statement on official letterhead from a licensed medical doctor, ophthalmologist, or optometrist.

  2. The letter must state the specific medical reason removal is impossible — not merely that you prefer to wear them.

  3. Submit the letter with your passport application at the time of photo submission.

  4. Even with an exemption, the photo must meet all biometric requirements: no glare, no shadows, eyes fully visible and unobstructed by frames.

If the photo fails the technical requirements despite the exemption, you will be asked to retake it. The exemption permits you to wear glasses — it does not exempt you from the image quality standards.

Contact Lenses and Tinted Lenses

Contact lenses occupy a separate category from eyeglasses, and the rules are consistent across all four countries.

  • Clear, non-tinted contact lenses are permitted in all countries without restriction. Because they do not introduce glare, shadows, or frame distortion, they pose no biometric interference. You do not need to disclose that you are wearing clear contacts.

  • Colored or cosmetic contact lenses that change the natural color of your eye are not permitted. The prohibition exists because eye color is recorded in passport data and used as an identification marker at some border control points. A photo that misrepresents your eye color creates a permanent discrepancy in your biometric record.

  • Transition lenses (photochromic lenses that darken in response to UV light) are banned in passport photos in all four countries. Even if the lenses appear clear indoors, they are classified as tinted lenses under passport photo rules. If you wear transitions as your only pair of glasses, remove them for the photo.

  • Theatrical or special-effects contact lenses — including lenses with patterns, unusual pupil shapes, or any non-standard appearance — are prohibited for the same reason as colored cosmetic lenses. 

Head Covering Rules in Passport Photos

Head coverings are evaluated differently from glasses. While glasses are prohibited by default (except in Canada), head coverings are permitted by default — provided they are worn for a genuine religious or medical reason and the covering does not interfere with the visibility of the face.

Allowed

Religious Head Coverings

Religious head coverings are permitted across all four countries. Accepted types include:

  • Hijab — worn by Muslim women; must be a plain, solid-colored fabric. The face from chin to hairline must be fully visible. No fabric may cross the forehead or cast a shadow over the nose bridge.

  • Turban — worn by Sikh men and women; the covering must be neat, symmetrical, and not create any shadow across the face.

  • Kippah (yarmulke) — typically small and positioned at the back of the head; generally does not interfere with visibility requirements.

  • Tichel or mitpachot — a Jewish head wrap; must be plain and not extend across the forehead.

  • Niqab or face veil — these are not permitted in any country for standard passport photos, as they cover the lower face and obstruct the landmarks required for biometric processing.

In the USA, the U.S. Department of State requires applicants wearing religious head coverings to submit a signed statement confirming the item is worn daily for religious reasons. Australia requires that the material be plain — no decorative patterns, embroidery, or textures — and that no shadows fall anywhere on the face.

Medical Head Coverings

Medical head coverings are permitted for documented conditions such as chemotherapy-related hair loss, alopecia, scalp conditions requiring protective covering, or recovery from head surgery. As with religious coverings, the full face must remain visible. Coverings worn for cosmetic reasons without a medical basis are not eligible for this exemption.

If the condition is temporary — such as post-operative wound coverage — it is worth waiting until the covering can be removed, if the timeline allows. A photo with a head covering on file may create verification difficulties later if the covering is no longer present when you travel.

What Is Never Allowed

The following are not permitted under any circumstances:

  • Fashion hats of any style (baseball caps, beanies, fedoras, wide-brim hats)

  • Bandanas or non-religious fabric wraps

  • Hair accessories that significantly alter the outline of the head

  • Coverings that obscure the hairline, forehead, or temples without a religious or medical basis

  • Any covering that casts a shadow on the face

  • Coverings with decorative patterns (prohibited specifically in Australia).
    If the condition is temporary — such as post-operative wound coverage — it is worth waiting until the covering can be removed, if the timeline allows. A photo with a head covering on file may create verification difficulties later if the covering is no longer present when you travel.

Visibility Requirements That Apply to Everyone

Regardless of whether you wear glasses, a head covering, or neither, the following facial features must be fully visible in every passport photo:

  • Both eyes — fully open, clearly visible, looking directly into the camera

  • Both eyebrows — completely unobscured by hair, frames, or fabric

  • The nose — full bridge and tip must be visible

  • The mouth — closed, with lips visible

  • The jawline — complete contour from ear to chin on both sides

  • The face outline — from the chin to the point where the covering or hairline begins

Ears are not required to be visible. This is a common myth. Neither the U.S. Department of State nor the ICAO standard requires ears to appear in a passport photo. Hair over the ears, head coverings that conceal the ears, and earrings that draw attention to the ear area are all acceptable, provided they do not interfere with the jawline or face outline.

Shadows: The Hidden Rejection Risk

Shadows are one of the single most common reasons passport photos are rejected — and they are almost entirely preventable with proper lighting setup.

For glasses wearers (primarily relevant in Canada, where glasses remain permitted), shadows cast by the frame — particularly from the bottom of thick frames falling across the upper cheek — will trigger rejection even if the photo meets all other requirements.

For head coverings, shadows present a more complex problem. A hijab or turban that sits close to the face can create a shadow along the jawline, across the forehead, or into the inner corners of the eyes. This occurs most often when the light source is overhead or off to one side.

How to eliminate shadows:

  1. Use diffuse, even front-facing lighting. Avoid single overhead bulbs or sunlight from a window casting strong shadows.

  2. Position yourself at least 50 cm from the background surface to prevent your head from casting a shadow behind you.

  3. If taking the photo at home, use two light sources at equal angles from both sides of your face to neutralize shadows.

  4. After taking the photo, zoom in on the eye corners and jawline area specifically to check for shadows.

  5. If using a hijab or turban, shoot a test frame and review it before the final submission.

Pre-Submission Checklist

Before submitting your passport photo, confirm each of the following:

  1. No glasses are present in the photo (unless you are in Canada with clear, glare-free lenses, or you hold a valid medical exemption with supporting documentation).

  2. No tinted lenses of any kind appear in the photo — including transition lenses, lightly tinted prescription lenses, or cosmetic contacts.

  3. If you wear a religious head covering, you have a signed daily-wear statement ready (required in the USA; confirm requirements for your country).

  4. If you wear a medical head covering, supporting documentation from your physician is attached to your application.

  5. The covering is plain material with no decorative patterns (required in Australia; best practice everywhere).

  6. Your eyes, eyebrows, nose, mouth, and jawline are all fully visible and unobscured.

  7. There are no shadows on your face — check the jaw line, forehead, and inner eye corners specifically.

  8. There is no shadow behind your head on the background.

  9. Your expression is neutral: eyes open, mouth closed, looking directly into the camera.

  10. The photo was taken within the past six months and accurately reflects your current appearance.

  11. Clear, non-tinted contact lenses are acceptable — confirm they are not cosmetically colored.

  12. You have reviewed the specific requirements for your country's passport office before final submission.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I Wear my Prescription Glasses in a US Passport Photo?

No. The U.S. Department of State has banned all eyeglasses from passport photos since November 2016. The ban applies to all applicants, including those who wear prescription glasses every day. The only exception is a documented medical condition that makes removal physically impossible, supported by a signed physician's statement. Vision correction needs alone do not qualify.

Is a Hijab Allowed in a Passport Photo?

Yes. A hijab is permitted in passport photos in the USA, UK, Canada, and Australia, provided it is worn for genuine religious reasons and the full face — from chin to the lower edge of the forehead — is clearly visible. In the USA, you must submit a signed statement confirming that you wear the hijab daily for religious reasons. In Australia, the material must be plain with no patterns and must not cast any shadow on the face.

Are Clear Contact Lenses Allowed in Passport Photos?

Yes. Clear, non-tinted contact lenses are permitted in all countries without restriction. They do not introduce glare, distortion, or biometric interference. Colored or cosmetic lenses that change your natural eye color are not permitted, as eye color is used as an identification reference in passport records.

Why are Transition Lenses Not Allowed Even if They Appear Clear Indoors?

Transition lenses are classified as tinted lenses under passport photo regulations, regardless of their appearance at the time the photo is taken. Because they can darken under UV exposure, the photo would not consistently represent your appearance across different lighting conditions. All four countries — the USA, the UK, Canada, and Australia — prohibit transition lenses.

Do My Ears Need to be Visible in a Passport Photo?

No. This is a widespread misconception. The U.S. Department of State does not require ears to be visible, and neither does the ICAO 9303 standard. Hair over the ears, head coverings that conceal the ears, and earrings are all acceptable, as long as the jawline and face outline remain fully visible.

What Happens if I Submit a Passport Photo With Glasses and My Application is Rejected?

Your application will be delayed, and you will need to submit a new, compliant photo before processing can continue. In some countries, any fees associated with the rejected application phase may not be refunded. If you are on a time-sensitive travel schedule, this delay can be significant. It is far more efficient to retake the photo before submission than to deal with a rejection after the fact.
Note: if your DV Lottery entry is rejected because of the glasses issue, you can only resubmit your entry the next year, with no exceptions.

Can I Wear a Kippah in My Passport Photo?

Yes. A kippah (yarmulke) is recognized as a religious head covering and is permitted in passport photos in all four countries. Because a kippah typically sits at the back or top of the head without covering the forehead, it rarely interferes with the required facial visibility. Confirm that it is not casting any shadows across the crown or forehead area.

requirements/green-card-photo-requiremen.content:
A green card photo is an official biometric image used by U.S. immigration authorities, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) and U.S. consular posts abroad, as part of the green card application process. It must meet strict U.S. Department of State specifications: exactly 2 × 2 inches, taken within the last six months against a plain white or off-white background, showing full face with neutral expression. Two identical copies printed on high-quality photo paper are required for your immigration interview. Our US green card photo guide converts a selfie into the 2 x 2 inch image you print for the interview.

This 2026 Guide covers the essential U.S. green card photo requirements you must follow to reduce the risk of delays or rejection of your application.

12 Essential 2026 Green Card Photo Requirements: Checklist

The US Department of State sets the official green card photo requirements, which, in turn, follow the biometric rules of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Document 9303. Including a photo that fully meets these specifications is crucial for the approval of your application. But you don't need to worry about that — you can make your green card photo online with PhotoGov: it automatically applies all official photo guidelines listed below. Work authorization documents are handled separately, and we prepare the employment authorization photo on its own page.

Specification

Requirement

1. Number of Photos

You must bring two identical printed photos to your green card interview at a U.S. embassy or consulate. Always follow the specific instructions provided by the embassy, consulate, or USCIS form you are using.

2. Recency

The picture must be taken within the last six months to ensure an accurate representation of the applicant's appearance. If the applicant has undergone a significant appearance change, such as plastic surgery, a more recent, new photo must be submitted.

3. Green Card Photo Size

2 × 2 inches (51 × 51 mm), with the head measuring 1–1⅜ inches (25–35 mm), or 50–69% of the photo's height, from the bottom of the chin to the top of the head. Check the exact measurements at the Department of State website.

4. Color

Only colored photos are accepted for a green card interview.

5. Background

Plain white or off-white background only. The background must be free from shadows, textures, or patterns.

6. Lighting

Professional, even lighting is required: the applicant's face must be clearly visible without any harsh shadows or bright spots. The light should be soft and balanced across the entire face, with naturally presented skin tones and hair color.

7. Positioning and Framing

The applicant must face the camera directly with their head centered and shoulders squared in the shot.

8. Facial Expression

Natural facial expression is required. The applicant's eyes must be open, and the mouth closed. No smiling, frowning, or any exaggerated expressions are allowed in the US immigrant visa photos.

9. Attire, Head Coverings, and Accessories

Wear everyday clothing in darker colors that clearly contrast with the background. Uniforms and camouflage are not permitted. Head coverings may be worn for religious reasons, provided they do not obscure any facial features or the hairline. If a head covering is worn for medical reasons, it must also not cover the face, and a medical statement signed by a doctor must be submitted with the application.

10. Glasses

Not allowed, including prescription glasses, colored contact lenses, tinted lenses, and sunglasses. If glasses cannot be taken off due to medical reasons, the frames cannot cover the eyes. The lenses must be free of glare or shadows, and a medical statement signed by a doctor must be submitted with the application.

11. Headphones and Hearing Aids

Headphones and wireless hands-free devices are not allowed in green card photos. The only exception is a hearing device worn daily that does not obstruct any facial features.

12. Print Quality

A photo must be printed professionally on matte or glossy photo‑quality paper without frames or decorative elements. Informal snapshots, photos cut out from magazines, low‑resolution kiosk prints, and full‑body images are not accepted. Digital source files must have enough resolution to produce a sharp 2 × 2 inch print without blur, visible pixels, or compression artifacts.

Green Card Printed and Digital Photo Explained

Winning the Diversity visa lottery requires attending a visa interview at a US embassy or consulate. Each selectee must bring two identical photographs that meet strict standards — square aspect ratio 2 × 2 inches (51 × 51 mm), professionally printed on photo-quality paper with a matte or glossy finish. No frames, borders, or decorative elements are permitted.

These photos can be produced from a digital file using professional printing services. The digital file must maintain square dimensions (600 × 600 to 1200 × 1200 pixels) at a 600 DPI resolution to ensure sharp, clear output without visible pixelation or compression artifacts when printed.

General appearance requirements remain identical for both formats: plain white or off-white background, neutral facial expression with both eyes open, no eyewear of any kind, and the photo taken within the last six months.

Where to Take Green Card Photo?

Many convenient locations in the US allow you to take your 2x2 green card photos. Choose the most suitable one, depending on your location and budget.

Pharmacies And Drug Stores

Pharmacy chains like Walgreens, CVS, and Rite Aid usually offer in‑store passport and green card photo services. This is a reliable choice, and there are many shops across all states.​

Shipping Centers

UPS and FedEx also provide photo services and take pictures for green card applications. It's especially convenient when there is an office nearby, or you need to pick up a parcel. ​

Post Offices

Post offices can handle photo services and, in some cases, accept green card applications in a single visit. Double-check with the nearest locations.

Photo Studios and Professional Photographers

Commercial studios and photographers offer professional green card photo services. This is often the most reliable option, as the quality is determined by the specialized lighting, setup, and the photographer’s experience.

Online Green Card Photo Editor

An online green card photo editor like PhotoGov allows you to take a green card photo from the comfort of your home. All you need is a laptop or a smartphone: simply click a selfie, upload it to the platform, and get a compliant image in seconds. A green card photo editor online is free in most cases, saving you money on a professional studio visit.

Taking Your Green Card Photo at Home

If you’d rather skip the hassle and the cost of a professional photo studio visit, you can easily take your own photo for a green card, using a smartphone or a digital camera. Create a simple setup and follow our expert tips for capturing a selfie — and then use the PhotoGov green card photo editor to adjust it to the US Department of State requirements, and ready for submission.

Prepare a simple setup for taking a green card photo. Find a well-lit spot, preferably by a window and with a plain white/off-white background. Check that nothing leaves shadows on the face or the backdrop.

Use a tripod or ask someone to take a shot. If using a tripod and a front camera, stand 5–7 feet (1.5–2 meters) away from it. If taking a selfie and using a front camera, keep it about 20 inches (50 cm) away from the face.

Follow dress code guidelines. Wear everyday clothes of darker colors, without large logos, lettering, or overly bright patterns. Religious head coverings are allowed if they do not obstruct facial features, but you cannot wear sunglasses, colored lenses, or tinted glasses in your green card photo.

Position yourself correctly. Stand or sit directly opposite the camera in an upright posture, with your head and shoulders square to the shot so they remain fully visible.

Keep a neutral expression. Look directly into the lens, keeping your eyes open and mouth closed. Don't smile or frown. Take multiple shots and choose the best one.

Browse PhotoGov and choose the document type — Green card. Upload your photo and wait about 30 seconds while our green card photo maker processes it, applying all the US Department of State requirements.

Save your green card 2x2 photo. After your portrait is processed, download the digital photo or the printable PDF file, and save it on your device. You're ready for an application process!

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the Official Green Card Photo Requirements for a Successful Application?

Green Card photos must meet strict biometric standards established by the Department of State and USCIS. The key specifications include:

  • Size: Exact 2 × 2 inches (51 × 51 mm) for physical prints
  • Head dimensions: 1–1⅜ inches (25–35 mm) from chin to crown
  • Background: Plain white or off-white, no shadows, patterns, or textures
  • Expression: Neutral — both eyes open, mouth closed, no smiling
  • Recency: Taken within the last 6 months
  • Print quality: Professional photo paper with matte or glossy finish
  • Color: Full color, no black and white​

What is the Green Card Photo Size?

The green card photo size must have a square aspect ratio of 2x2 inches (51x51 mm). The head must be measuring between 1 and 1 3/8 inches (22–35 mm) from the bottom of the chin to the top of the head.

How Many Photos to Submit With a Green Card Application?

You need to bring two identical 2 × 2 inch photos to your immigrant visa interview. For applications filed inside the U.S., the number of photos and exact requirements are specified in the instructions for Form I‑485 and any other USCIS forms in your case.

Is Green Card Photo Same as Passport?

Yes. The official requirements for a green card and the US passport photos are identical:

  • Passport and green card photo size: 2x2 inches, head size between 1 and 1 1/38 inches (22-35 mm).
  • Background: Plain white or off-white.
  • Facial expression: Neutral, eyes open, mouth closed.
  • Attire: Daily clothes, no military or camouflage wear. Head coverings can be worn only for religious or medical reasons and cannot obstruct facial features.
  • Glasses: Do not wear glasses or tinted lenses in the photo.

What are the Rules for Clothing, Background, and Facial Expression in a Green Card Photo?

Your appearance in a Green Card photo is subject to specific regulations designed to ensure consistent biometric identification:

Clothing:

  • Everyday clothing in solid colors
  • No uniforms, camouflage, or military attire
  • No white clothing that blends with the background
  • Religious clothing is allowed if worn daily

Background:

  • Plain white or off-white only
  • No cream, grey, or blue tints
  • No objects, textures, or patterns in the frame

Facial expression:

  • Neutral expression is mandatory
  • Both eyes must be fully open
  • The mouth must be closed
  • No smiling, frowning, or raised eyebrows​

What are the Green Card Photo Requirements for Glasses, Head Coverings, and Hairstyles?

Accessories and personal appearance elements must comply with strict visibility standards:

Glasses:

  • Not permitted for green card photos
  • No exceptions, even with medical documentation

Head coverings:

  • Only for religious or medical reasons
  • Must not obscure hairline, eyebrows, or facial contours
  • Cannot cast shadows on the face
  • Medical reasons require a signed doctor's statement

Hairstyles:

  • Must not cover eyes or eyebrows
  • Full hairline visible
  • Both ears visible
  • No headphones or wireless devices​

What Resolution and File Format Should My Green Card Photo Have for Online Submission?

Digital photos used for green card‑related applications (such as DV Lottery entries or files prepared for printing) require specific formatting:

  • Format: JPEG (.jpg) only
  • Dimensions: 600 × 600 to 1200 × 1200 pixels (square)
  • File size: Maximum 240 KB
  • Color depth: Minimum 24-bit sRGB
  • Head height: 50–69% of total image height
  • Compression: No visible artifacts or quality loss

Green card photos, however, are only submitted in person during an interview. You must bring two identical 2x2 photos, printed on high-quality photo paper.

How Can I Check if My Digital Photo Meets Green Card Photo Specifications Before Submitting?

Use the PhotoGov green card photo checker. The service offers comprehensive photo validation specifically designed for DV Lottery applications. Upload your image to the system — the algorithm automatically verifies:

  • Dimensional compliance and head-to-frame proportions
  • Background color (plain white or off-white)
  • Absence of shadows and proper lighting
  • Neutral facial expression and open eyes
  • Technical specifications: JPEG format, file size, sRGB color profile.

The system provides instant results with specific details on any non-compliance. When using PhotoGov's digital tool to create a photo from scratch, you receive a guarantee of compliance with Department of State requirements. If your photo is rejected at the embassy due to technical errors, PhotoGov provides a free retake or full refund after you contact support with the rejection notice.

Keep in mind that you must bring two identical printed photos for your green card interview. Digital uploads are only required for the DV visa lottery entries.

How Close Should My Face Be in a Green Card Photo and What Proportion of the Image Should It Cover?

Your head must measure between 1 and 1 3/8 inches (25 to 35 mm) from the bottom of the chin to the top of the head. The head should occupy approximately 50 percent of the total photo height, centered horizontally within the frame. Position your eyes between 1 1/8 and 1 3/8 inches (28 to 35 mm) from the bottom edge of the photo. Your face must be fully visible, facing the camera directly without tilting or turning.

What Background Color and Lighting Conditions are Required for a Compliant Green Card Photo?

Proper background and illumination are essential for biometric recognition:

Background color:

  • Plain white or off-white (cream or grey tints are rejected)
  • No shadows on the wall or behind the applicant
  • No textures, patterns, or gradients
  • Uniform color throughout

Lighting:

  • Even, diffused illumination from multiple sources
  • No shadows under nose, chin, or around ears
  • No flash glare or red-eye
  • Natural light or soft artificial light preferred

Where Can I Get a Green Card Photo Taken That Fully Complies With All Official Requirements Near Me?

Several nationwide providers offer compliant 2 × 2-inch passport-style services:

Pharmacies and retail stores offer convenient in-person service. Walgreens, CVS, and Rite Aid typically charge $15–$18 for two prints, while Walmart provides a more economical option at $8-$12.

Shipping and postal centers — UPS Store and FedEx Office charge $12-$15, but require an appointment for passport photo services.

Professional photography studios offer the highest quality assurance for green card photos, with sessions typically costing $25-50. Commercial photographers provide controlled lighting, proper backdrops, and precise framing that ensures exact 2 × 2-inch dimensions and correct head proportions.

Online green card photo-making tools. A passport photo maker, PhotoGov, is a great option for those who prefer to save time and money, skipping a visit to a studio. The system converts your selfie into a compliant green card photo in under 30 seconds. It automatically adjusts your background to plain white/off-white, crops the image to exact 2 × 2 inch dimensions, and verifies that your head occupies the correct proportion of the frame. Every photo is validated against Department of State standards before download.

Are there Different Green Card Photo Requirements for Children and Infants?

Yes. Generally, green card photos of children follow the same specifications as adult pictures — 2 x 2 in size, plain white or off-white background, and should be taken within the past 6 months.

However, there are exceptions for infants under one year old:

  • Their eyes may be partially or fully closed, and they do not need to look directly at the camera.
  • A parent may support the infant's head from behind as long as their hands remain completely out of the frame.
  • The baby can be laid down on a white sheet and photographed from directly above, or when seated upright in a white car seat.
  • Toys, bottles, pacifiers, other people, or visible hands can’t be present in a shot.

Can I Retouch or Edit My Green Card Photo, and What Modifications are Allowed Under the Requirements?

Digital alterations are strictly limited to maintain biometric accuracy. You cannot use filters or beauty modes, skin smoothing, teeth whitening, red-eye removal, background replacement, cropping that alters head proportions, or brightness adjustments that change your natural appearance.

Allowed modifications:

  • Minor brightness adjustments preserving natural skin tone
  • Conversion to the required square format without image stretching
  • File size compression that preserves image quality

Is My Smartphone Photo Good Enough for a Green Card Application, and How Do I Format It Correctly?

Yes. Modern smartphones are good enough to capture green card photos that meet USCIS requirements — if used correctly:

  • Ensure your device has a camera with at least 12 megapixels
  • Shoot in natural daylight or with even indoor lighting
  • Position yourself approximately 4 to 6 feet from the camera to avoid distortion, and never use digital zoom.
  • The image must be sharp, properly exposed without shadows on the face, and show true skin tones.

To format your photo to the green card photo specifications, use PhotoGov. The platform automatically converts your photo to the required 2 × 2 inch dimensions, adjusts the background to plain white/off-white, verifies that head proportions occupy 50 percent of the frame, and validates technical parameters against official standards. Upload your original high-resolution JPEG directly from your phone, and avoid editing apps or filters before submission to the platform.

Where Can I Upload My Picture to Verify if It Satisfies All Green Card Photo Requirements Before I Apply?

Use an online tool like PhotoGov. It has a built-in verification system for green card photos. Upload any image from your smartphone or camera, and the algorithm automatically analyzes dimensions, background color, head proportions, eye positioning, and lighting conditions against Department of State specifications. The system flags any non-compliance issues before you download the final file. If embassy or USCIS staff reject your PhotoGov photo due to technical non-compliance, customer support will review your case and provide either detailed correction instructions, unlimited free retakes, or a full refund.

What are the Most Common Reasons Green Card Photos Get Rejected and How Can I Avoid Them?

Green card photos are rejected for failing to meet the US Department of State technical specifications. The most common reasons include:

  • Incorrect photo dimensions – Image larger or smaller than 2 × 2 inches (51 × 51 mm) or not having a square aspect ratio
  • Incorrect head size – Head measuring less than 1 inch or more than 1 3/8 inches from chin to crown, or occupying less than 50 percent of the frame height
  • Poor print quality – Visible printer dots, pixelation, blurry details, or not professionally printed on non-photo paper
  • Low resolution – Images printed at less than 300 DPI or appearing grainy and indistinct
  • Non-compliant background – Grey, cream shades instead of plain white or off-white, visible shadows, wall textures, or patterns behind the subject
  • Improper facial expression – Smiling, frowning, raised eyebrows, or head tilted away from direct camera alignment
  • Wearing glasses – All eyeglasses are prohibited in Green Card photos; they must be removed before taking the photo
  • Unauthorized digital alterations – Filters, beauty modes, skin smoothing, teeth whitening, background replacement, or cropping that distort proportions
  • Shadow interference – Shadows cast on the face, background, or behind the head from improper lighting
  • Foreign objects in the photos of children — Pacifiers, parents’ hands, furniture in the shot, may lead to rejection.

To prevent rejection, print your photo professionally at 600 DPI on photo-quality paper, verify sharp focus without pixelation or visible printer patterns, and validate your final image or create it from scratch through PhotoGov, which checks all technical parameters against Department of State standards.

mainEntity.name: What are the Official Green Card Photo Requirements for a Successful Application?

acceptedAnswer.text: Green Card photos must meet strict biometric standards established by the Department of State and USCIS. Key specifications include: size of exactly 2 x 2 inches (51 x 51 mm) for printed photos; head dimensions between 1 and 1 3/8 inches (25–35 mm) from chin to crown; a plain white or off-white background with no shadows, patterns, or textures; a neutral facial expression with both eyes open and mouth closed; the photo taken within the last 6 months; professional-quality printing on matte or glossy photo paper; and full colour with no black-and-white images.

mainEntity.name: What is the Green Card Photo Size?

acceptedAnswer.text: A Green Card photo must have a square aspect ratio of 2 x 2 inches (51 x 51 mm). The head must measure between 1 and 1 3/8 inches (22–35 mm) from the bottom of the chin to the top of the head.

mainEntity.name: How Many Photos to Submit With a Green Card Application?

acceptedAnswer.text: You must bring two identical 2 x 2 inch photos to your immigrant visa interview. For applications filed inside the United States, the number of photos and exact specifications are given in the instructions to Form I-485 and any additional USCIS forms included in your case.

mainEntity.name: Is Green Card Photo Same as Passport?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The official requirements for US Green Card and US passport photos are the same. Both require a 2 x 2 inch image with a head size between 1 and 1 3/8 inches (22–35 mm), a plain white or off-white background, a neutral expression with eyes open and mouth closed, everyday clothing without military or camouflage patterns, and head coverings only for religious or medical reasons that do not obscure facial features. Glasses and tinted lenses are not allowed.

mainEntity.name: What are the Rules for Clothing, Background, and Facial Expression in a Green Card Photo?

acceptedAnswer.text: Clothing must be everyday wear in solid colours, with no uniforms, camouflage, or military attire and no white tops that blend into the background. Religious clothing is permitted if worn daily. The background must be plain white or off-white only, without cream, grey, or blue tints and without objects, textures, or patterns. A neutral expression is mandatory, with both eyes fully open, mouth closed, and no smiling, frowning, or raised eyebrows.

mainEntity.name: What are the Green Card Photo Requirements for Glasses, Head Coverings, and Hairstyles?

acceptedAnswer.text: Glasses are not permitted in Green Card photos and there are no exceptions, even for medical reasons. Head coverings are allowed only for religious or medical reasons and must not obscure the hairline, eyebrows, or facial contours, and must not cast shadows on the face; medical use requires a signed doctor's statement. Hairstyles must not cover the eyes or eyebrows, the hairline should be visible, both ears should be visible, and headphones or wireless devices are not allowed.

mainEntity.name: What Resolution and File Format Should My Green Card Photo Have for Online Submission?

acceptedAnswer.text: Digital images used for Green Card–related applications, such as DV Lottery entries or files prepared for printing, must be in JPEG format with a square aspect ratio between 600 x 600 and 1200 x 1200 pixels, a maximum file size of 240 KB, and a minimum 24-bit sRGB colour depth. The head height should be 50–69 percent of the total image height and compression must not introduce visible artefacts. For the Green Card interview itself, two identical 2 x 2 inch photos printed on high-quality photo paper are required.

mainEntity.name: How Close Should My Face Be in a Green Card Photo and What Proportion of the Image Should It Cover?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your head must measure between 1 and 1 3/8 inches (25–35 mm) from the bottom of the chin to the top of the head, occupying about 50 percent of the total photo height and centred horizontally. Your eyes should be positioned between 1 1/8 and 1 3/8 inches (28–35 mm) from the bottom edge of the photo. Your face must be fully visible, looking straight at the camera without tilting or turning.

mainEntity.name: What Background Color and Lighting Conditions are Required for a Compliant Green Card Photo?

acceptedAnswer.text: The background must be plain white or off-white, with no cream or grey tints, no textures, patterns, gradients, or visible shadows behind the applicant, and a uniform colour across the frame. Lighting must be even and diffused, with no shadows under the nose, chin, or around the ears, and no flash glare or red-eye. Natural light or soft artificial light from multiple sources is preferred.

For infants under one year, eyes may be partially or fully closed and they do not need to look directly at the camera. Babies can be photographed lying on a white sheet from above or seated upright in a white car seat, but toys, bottles, pacifiers, other people, and visible hands are not allowed in the photo.

requirements/india-visa-photo.content:
Planning a trip to India? When applying for a visa, you must upload a compliant photograph that follows all India visa photo requirements — a square image with a plain light-colored or white background, 350 x 350 to 1,000 x 1,000 pixel dimensions with the head measuring 1 to 1-3/8 inches (25 to 35 mm) from chin to hairline, saved as a JPEG of 10 KB – 1 MB for an e-Visa and

10 – 300 KB for a regular visa. 

This Guide covers all India visa photo requirements for 2026, so you can submit your application successfully. Have a nice trip!

Source: Bureau of Immigration, Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India

11 Essential India Visa Photo Requirements: a Checklist

Indian photo requirements are published on the official visa and e-Visa portal operated by the Bureau of Immigration under India's Ministry of Home Affairs. Specifications in the table below apply to the standard online upload for both the regular visa and the e-Visa. Follow them exactly: a file that misses one or more official specs may get automatically rejected by the portal.

Requirement

Details

1. File Format

JPEG only. 

2. File Size

10 KB – 1 MB for an e-Visa application; 10 – 300 KB for a regular visa application.

3. Photo Dimensions

350 x 350 to 1,000 x 1,000 pixels.

4. Background

Plain light colored or white background.

5. Framing

Full-face, front view, centered in the frame, showing the entire head from the top of the hair to the bottom of the chin.

6. Head Size

The head must measure 1 to 1-3/8 inches (25 to 35 mm), from the bottom of the chin to the top of the hair.

7. Facial expression

Neutral facial expression. Eyes open, mouth closed.

8. Glasses

The official eVisa website requires a photo "without spectacles." 

9. Headwear and accessories

Remove any headwear and accessories obstructing facial features or fully covering your neck (scarf). Only medical (with a relevant letter from a medical provider) or religious headwear worn daily is accepted. 

10. Lighting 

Even, shadow-free lighting on the face and background — no shadows, textures, glare, or reflections.

11. Borders, frames, decorative artefacts

The photo must be cropped to the edge — no frames, borders, or any decorative elements are allowed.

Acceptable Indian Visa Photo Examples

Unacceptable Indian Visa Photo Examples

India Visa Photo Size and Pixel Dimensions Explained

India visa photo is a digital upload — its size is measured in pixels. The regular visa instructions on the official visa portal require photos of a minimum of 350 x 350 pixels and a maximum of 1,000 x 1,000 pixels. A rectangular crop, even a photo that is just a few pixels off square, will fail the upload check.

The head, measured from the bottom of your chin to the top of your hair, needs to fill 1 to 1-3/8 inches (25 to 35 mm). Standing too close to the camera pushes the head measurement over the limit; standing too far back leaves too much background, making the face too small for biometric identification. The best way to shoot a proper photo is to stand about three feet away from the camera, placed on a tripod at eye level. 

India e-Visa vs Regular Visa Photo Requirements: What's Different

Most travelers apply for an Indian visa through the e-Visa system. It covers tourist, business, medical, conference, and several other short-stay categories entirely online. A smaller group of applicants, mainly those filing for employment, student, journalist, or research visas, use the regular (sticker) visa route instead. Initially, the application is submitted via the official visa portal too, but it requires a printed application submitted through an Indian mission or its outsourced visa partner. The photo file, therefore, must follow a slightly different set of requirements.

Comparison Table: e-Visa vs Paper Visa Sticker Photo

Aspect

e-Visa 

Regular Visa

File size

10 KB to 1 MB

10 KB to 300 KB

Format

JPEG

JPEG

Where it's uploaded

Directly in the e-Visa application on indianvisaonline.gov.in

On the same portal, then the printed application and photo are submitted with your documents

Glasses

eVisa portal requires photos "without spectacles" 

Though authorities don’t specify the glasses rule for regular visas, we recommend removing them for the photo

Typical use case

Tourist, business, medical, conference, and other short-stay categories

Employment, student, journalist, research, and other categories outside the e-Visa list

If you already have a compliant e-Visa photo and later need to switch to a regular visa application, check the file size again before you resubmit it. A photo saved at 800 KB clears the e-Visa limit but is too large for the regular visa upload: you would need to compress it before the portal accepts it. 

India Visa Photo Background, Lighting, and Framing Rules

The official Indian visa portal requires a plain light-colored or white background with even lighting on the face and background, free of shadows. The framing instructions ask for a front-facing headshot, with the full head visible from the top of the hair to the bottom of the chin. A tilted head, a photo taken from slightly above or below eye level, or a stray white frame left in by an editing app are all common reasons for rejection.

India Visa Photo Rules: Glasses and Facial Expression

On the official Indian visa portal, glasses are explicitly addressed only for the e-Visa, where the instructions require the photo to be taken "without spectacles." We recommend following the same rule for a visa sticker application too — it's the safer choice, since even prescription glasses with clear lenses can produce glare or reflections that interfere with biometric identification.

The international rule for facial expression in ID photos is set by the International Civil Aviation Organization Document 9303. It requires a neutral facial expression with both eyes open and mouth closed. Exaggerated expressions, including a wide smile, can compromise the biometric scans. Therefore, when making an Indian visa photo, maintain a calm, natural expression — it keeps your photo consistent both for automated identification systems and border officers. 

According to international visa photo standards, all head coverings must be taken off, unless worn for religious or medical reasons. If you wear a religious head covering daily, keep your full face visible from the bottom of your chin to the top of your hairline, following the general framing rule. Check with your Indian mission or the eVisa Help Desk at indian-evisa@gov.in or at +91 82 7808 7808 beforehand if you have a specific concern.

India Visa Photo Rules for Children and Infants

Every applicant, including an infant, needs their own visa and their own photo. The portal applies the same specifications to every applicant regardless of age. So, a child's photo follows the same file format, size, background, and framing rules as an adult's.

The practical challenge is getting an infant or toddler to sit still, front-facing, with both eyes open, against a plain background. When taking a photo of your infant at home, lay them on a plain light-colored sheet or blanket and photograph from directly above, with the camera level and the baby's face centered in the frame. For a baby who can sit up, a car seat or high chair pushed against a bare wall works, keeping straps, hands, and toys clear of the final crop. Take a longer sequence of shots, twenty or more, and pick the sharpest frame with both eyes open and fingers clear of the face.

Where to Apply for an India Visa Photo: e-Visa Portal and Missions Abroad

The e-Visa application, including the photo upload, is completed entirely on indianvisaonline.gov.in. The Bureau of Immigration has issued a public advisory naming it as the only correct website for the e-Visa, after several lookalike sites were found copying the government's design to collect fees and personal documents from applicants. Before you upload an Indian visa photo, check that the address bar reads indianvisaonline.gov.in exactly.


A regular visa application starts on the same portal, but the printed form, photo, and passport are then submitted in person or through an outsourced visa application center that handles document collection for Indian missions in the United States and elsewhere. If a visa center or a travel agent quotes you a photo rule that conflicts with what is published on the government portal, the portal is the version that governs your application.

The Bureau of Immigration has also stated plainly that "Government of India has not authorized any agent or intermediary to charge any fee for facilitation of emergency / express Visa/eVisa." A third party can help you fill out paperwork, though the Bureau of Immigration alone sets the rules for your visa timeline and the photo specifications.

Route

Photo Upload Channel

Visa Purpose

e-Visa

Uploaded directly on indianvisaonline.gov.in

Tourist, business, medical, conference, and other eligible short-stay categories

Regular visa

Uploaded to the portal, then the printed application is submitted through an Indian mission or a third-party visa center

Employment, student, journalist, research, and categories outside the e-Visa list

How to Take an India Visa Photo at Home: 5 Easy Steps


A home setup is enough to produce a compliant India visa photo:

  1. Place your phone on a tripod against a light-colored or white wall, preferably by the window. Take the photo in daylight only. Always use the rear camera on your phone for sharper detail than the front-facing one typically captures. Set up a timer.

  2. Remove your glasses, heavy accessories, and non-medical or non-religious headwear.

  3. Stand about three feet from the wall, keep a neutral expression looking directly into the camera.

  4. Take a few shots and choose the best one for your Indian visa.

  5. Use a reputable online tool to create an application-ready photo. For example, PhotoGov's India visa photo maker automates the cropping and background steps: it resizes your uploaded selfie to a square file, checks the pixel dimensions against the range published on indianvisaonline.gov.in, and adjusts the background color. The tool creates a ready-to-submit digital file of the right size, crop, and dimensions that you can download in under 30 seconds.

Common Reasons an India Visa Photo Gets Rejected

An upload that fails even one of the published parameters gets rejected by the portal, and you have to fix the file and try again before your application can move forward.

Reason for rejection

How to fix it

Wrong dimensions

Crop the image to a square before you save it

Wrong file size

Compress or resave the JPEG until it falls between 10 KB and 300 KB (regular visa) or 10 KB and 1 MB (e-Visa)

Wrong file format

Save the file as a JPEG (.jpg), the only format the portal accepts

Wrong background color, shadows, or textures

Reshoot against a plain light-colored or white wall with even lighting

Glasses, accessories, or headwear

Remove your glasses, large accessories, and headwear (unless medical or religious)  and reshoot

Wrong head size

Reframe so your head measures 1 to 1-3/8 inches (25 to 35 mm), and reshoot

Border or frame 

Re-export the file cropped flush to the edge

A file size or border problem can usually be fixed with the same photo. A shadow, a tilted head, or visible glasses on an e-Visa photo generally calls for starting over with a new shot.

How to Check Your India Visa Photo Before You Submit

Since the photo is uploaded as part of the online application, the only real test is whether the file passes the portal's own checks on the first try. Before you upload, confirm the file is a JPEG, is square, falls within the 350 x 350 and 1,000 x 1,000 pixel range, and is sized 10 KB to 1 MB for eVisa and 10 KB to 300 KB for a regular visa. The background must be white or light-colored, and the image must be free of shadows, glare, and textures. You must face the camera directly with a neutral expression, mouth closed and eyes open. To be sure, use a reliable online visa photo checker.

Your India Visa Photo Is Ready: What's Next?

Your India visa photo is ready. Before you submit your application, here's what to check next.

  • Review the rest of your application. The photo is only one requirement — make sure your passport is valid for at least six months beyond your intended date of entry, your application form is complete, and any supporting documents are ready to upload.

  • Check if other Indian documents need a photo too. If you're also applying for an Indian passport, the photo standard is different — see PhotoGov's guide to Indian passport photo requirements for the separate 35×45 mm specification.

  • Applying for another country as well? Photo specs vary by destination. PhotoGov helps you create submission-ready US visa photo, Canadian visa photo, Schengen visa photo, and many more — each automatically adjusted to current official requirements.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Size is an Indian Visa Photo?

The Indian visa photo must be square, between 350 x 350 and 1,000 x 1,000 pixels, with the head measuring 1 to 1-3/8 inches (25 to 35 mm) from chin to hairline.

What is the File Size Limit for an India e-Visa Photo?

Between 10 KB and 1 MB. A regular (non-e-Visa) application requires a smaller range of 10 KB to 300 KB — always double-check the official source (indianvisaonline.gov.in) before applying.

Can I Wear Glasses in My India Visa Photo?

No. The official e-Visa instructions specifically require the photo to be taken "without spectacles," and we recommend following the same rule for a regular (sticker) visa.

What Color is the Background for Indian Visa Photo?

A plain light colored or white background, evenly lit and free of shadows on the face or the background. A light gray or pale wall is acceptable as long as it is even and free of texture.

How Recent Must My India Visa Photo Be?

Use a current photo that matches your appearance at the time of application, and check for an exact requirement with your Indian mission for your visa category.

Do I Need to Submit a Printed Photo, or is Digital Enough?

For an Indian e-Visa, you must submit your photo online — so only a digital photo. For a regular visa, the photo is uploaded to the same portal, and the printed application is then submitted through an Indian mission or a third-party visa center.

Do the Same India Visa Photo Rules Apply to Children?

Yes. The Bureau of Immigration applies the same Indian visa photo specifications to every applicant regardless of age, so a child's photo follows the same format, size, background, and framing rules as an adult's — plain light-colored or white background, 350 x 350 to 1,000 x 1,000 pixels, head measuring 1 to 1-3/8 inches (25 to 35 mm) from chin to hairline, saved as a JPEG of 10 – 300 KB for a regular visa or up to 1 MB for an e-Visa. 

What File Format is Required for an Indian Visa Photo?

JPEG only. The Indian visa upload will reject PNG, HEIC, and other digital photo formats, so make sure you’re creating the right file. If you don’t know how to convert your Android or iPhone photo into a JPEG, use PhotoGov’s India Visa Maker — the tool will automatically prepare an application-ready JPEG with the right proportions and digital file specs.

Do e-Visa and Regular India Visa Photos Share the Same Requirements?

Yes and no. Both an eVisa and a regular Indian visa require a square photo within a 350 x 350 to 1,000 x 1,000 pixel limit, taken against a white or light-colored background and saved as a JPEG. But the file size for a photo upload differs: 10 KB to 1 MB for the e-Visa, and 10 KB to 300 KB for the regular visa.

Why Does My Indian Visa Photo Keep Getting Rejected on Upload?

The most common causes for Indian visa photo rejection are: 

  • A non-square crop falling outside the 350 x 350 to 1,000 x 1,000 pixel range
    A file outside the size limit of 10 – 300 KB for a regular visa or up to 1 MB for an e-Visa

  • Non-white or non-light-colored background

  • Shadows or textures in the background

  • Applicant wears glasses 

  • Non-religious headwear.

Check each item against the checklist in this guide before you reapply.

Is indianvisaonline.gov.in the Only Official Site for an India Visa Photo?

Yes. The Bureau of Immigration’s only official website is indianvisaonline.gov.in. Do not try to apply for an Indian visa through any other commercial websites.

Can I Use the Same Photo for My Indian Visa and my Passport?

No. We don’t recommend doing so, as each document type has specific requirements. However, if you’re using online photo-making tools to create a photo for your document, you can use one source image if it’s of sufficient quality. 

What is the Difference Between an India Visa Photo and an Indian Passport Photo?

An India visa photo and an Indian passport photo are part of applications for two completely different documents, issued by different authorities. An India visa photo is submitted by a foreign national applying to enter India; it must be square, sized between 350×350 and 1,000×1,000 pixels. An Indian passport photo, on the other hand, is submitted by an Indian citizen to Passport Seva, following a 35×45 mm photo size and a different set of requirements — you can learn them from our detailed Indian passport photo requirements guide.

requirements/indian-pan-card-photo.content:
Applying for a Permanent Account Number (PAN) in India and unsure which photo belongs on the form? Prepare two matching recent colour photographs in the 3.5 x 4.5 cm (35 × 45 mm) format, both taken against a plain white background. One photo must present your signature or a left-thumb impression across the edge; the second stays clear — it’s the portrait that will be printed on your PAN card. This format serves other applications too: an Indian passport size photo 35x45 mm can be prepared with our online maker.

This guide takes you through every current PAN card photo requirement, from size and background to placement, signing and submission, with direct links to the official forms and authorised application channels.

Indian Permanent Account Number Card Photo Explained

A Permanent Account Number, or PAN, is a ten-character alphanumeric identifier issued by India’s Income Tax Department. If you are applying as an individual, the form asks for two matching photographs, and each print does a different job. The left image links your signature or left-thumb impression to the application, while the right image supplies the portrait reproduced on the PAN card. Travel documents use other specifications: an India e visa photo is prepared in the 2 x 2 inch format on a separate page.

The left-hand box of the form is for the photo crossed by your signature or left-thumb impression, with the mark continuing onto the form. The right-hand box is for your portrait to be used on the card. 

The form you will use for PAN application depends on your citizenship. Indian citizens apply on Form No. 93, while applicants who hold another citizenship use Form No. 95. Applications can be filed online through Protean eGov or UTIITSL, or in person at an authorised Protean PAN Centre or UTIITSL PAN Centre. Instant e-PAN is a separate Aadhaar e-KYC service and uses the photograph held in the Aadhaar record. Applicants holding OCI status often need an OCI passport photo online as well, in the format that document requires.

12 Key Indian PAN Card Photo Requirements: a Checklist

The Income Tax Department sets the current PAN photo rules for individual applicants in the official Form No. 93 and Form No. 95 guidelines. The table below consolidates the full specifications for a clean, correctly attached submission.

Parameter

Requirement

1. Applicant scope

Individual applicants, including minors and applicants using a Representative Assessee, provide photographs with Form No. 93 or Form No. 95.

2. Number of photos

Two matching recent colour photographs.

3. PAN photo size

3.5 × 4.5 cm (35 × 45 mm).

4. Orientation

Portrait orientation.

5. Colour

Natural colour with clear, accurate facial detail.

6. Background

Plain white background.

7. Recency

A recent photograph that reflects the applicant’s current appearance.

8. Image clarity

Sharp focus, clear facial features, balanced exposure, and a clean print surface.

9. Attachment method

Photo adhesive secures each print inside the designated box.

10. Left photograph

Signature or left-thumb impression crosses the photograph and continues onto the form.

11. Right photograph

A clear, unobstructed image free from signatures, stamps, and other marks.

12. Thumb-impression authentication

A Magistrate, Notary Public, Oath Commissioner, or Gazetted Officer attests a left-thumb impression under official seal and stamp.

Prepare the correct image with PhotoGov’s PAN card photo maker, download a print-ready file in the 4.5 × 3.5 cm (35 × 45 mm) format, and print two matching copies. Then attach and sign the photos according to the form instructions.

India’s New PAN Application Photo Rule: What Changed in 2026

India introduced a new set of PAN application forms under the Income-tax Rules, 2026. New applications filed from Apr 1, 2026 use Form No. 93 for individual Indian citizens and Form No. 95 for individuals who are citizens of another country.

Current Forms 93 and 95 require two recent colour photos in the 4.5 × 3.5 cm (35 × 45 mm) format. The earlier Form 49A and Form 49AA used the smaller 3.5 × 2.5 cm (35 × 25 mm) format. Use the current 35 × 45 mm size for applications filed under the 2026 rules.

How to Submit Photos with Form No. 93 or Form No. 95

Use the form that matches your citizenship category: No. 93 if you are a citizen of India, No. 95 if you are a citizen of another country. Each form provides two portrait boxes sized for 4.5 × 3.5 cm prints.

  • Prepare two matching recent colour photographs with a white background.

  • Trim each print to 35 × 45 mm.

  • Apply photo adhesive evenly and place both photographs squarely inside the printed boxes.

  • Sign or place the left thumb impression across the left photograph so the mark extends onto the form.

  • Keep the right photograph clean and fully visible.

  • Place the final signature or left-thumb impression inside the declaration box on the last page.

  • Arrange official attestation for a left-thumb impression through a Magistrate, Notary Public, Oath Commissioner, or Gazetted Officer, with the official seal and stamp.

Applicants using an online PAN application with a physical-document submission mode follow the acknowledgement instructions shown by the selected service. The acknowledgement carries the photographs, signatures, and supporting documents for dispatch through the stated channel.

Indian PAN Card Photo Background: White

The current Income Tax Department guidelines specify a white background for both photographs. Use a smooth, evenly lit white surface that creates clear separation around the head, hair, and shoulders.

Stand about one metre in front of the background and direct soft light toward the face. This setup keeps the background bright, the facial features clear, and the skin tone natural. Frame a straightforward head-and-shoulders portrait with the face centred and the camera at eye level.

The official PAN forms focus on identification quality rather than a published biometric head-height percentage. Give the face generous space within the 35 × 45 mm frame while keeping the complete head and upper shoulders visible.

Glasses in Indian PAN Card Photos

For the clearest result, remove glasses before capture. This keeps both eyes fully visible and prevents lens glare. Tinted lenses, sunglasses, or prescription glasses with heavy frames are generally not allowed on ID photos. If you must wear glasses, make sure they have transparent lenses, and look directly into the camera.

Where to Get a Compliant Indian PAN Card Photo in 2026

A paper PAN application requires two photo prints. You can prepare the photo at home, using an online photo-making tool, get it done by a professional photographer, at a local photo studio, or use a self-service booth. Other Indian forms use the same 35 x 45 mm portrait, and our page on the Indian driving licence photo size explains the RTO version.

How to Prepare a PAN Card Photo with PhotoGov

PhotoGov is a convenient option when you don't want to spend time and money on a studio visit. Start with a clear, front-facing smartphone photo taken against a simple light surface. Upload it to PhotoGov and select the 35 × 45 mm Indian PAN Card format.

The tool prepares the white background, crop, and printable layout for the required physical size. Download the finished file and order two identical colour prints at a local print shop. The result is a ready-to-attach pair of photos: the left print receives the signature or thumb impression, and the right one remains clear for the card portrait. Choosing a different document type produces an India passport size photo from the same portrait.

Indian PAN Card Photos for Minors

The Form No. 93 and Form No. 95 guidelines apply the same photo requirement to every individual applicant, including minors. Prepare two recent colour photographs with a white background in the 4.5 × 3.5 cm format.

Choose a calm moment and photograph the child from directly in front. Use an eye-level camera, even light, a smooth white background, and a frame containing only the child. For a baby, place the infant on a smooth white sheet and hold the camera directly above the face.

A minor’s application uses a Representative Assessee where the form requires one. Complete the photograph and signature or left-thumb impression fields according to the current form, and arrange official attestation when a thumb impression is used.

Common Reasons for Indian PAN Card Photo Rejection

PAN application review focuses on the form, portrait clarity, photograph placement, and authentication marks. These issues create the highest risk of a deficient submission:

  1. Old 35 × 25 mm format: prepare new 35 × 45 mm prints for the current Form No. 93 or Form No. 95.

  2. Single photograph: attach two matching photographs in the two designated boxes.

  3. Coloured or textured background: use a smooth white background with even illumination.

  4. Soft focus or low contrast: select a sharp portrait with clear facial detail and natural colour.

  5. Staple or clip marks: secure each print with photo adhesive.

  6. Signature placed entirely inside the left image: extend the signature or left-thumb impression across the photo-form boundary.

  7. Mark on the right image: reserve the right photograph as a clean, unobstructed portrait.

  8. Unattested thumb impression: obtain the required official attestation, seal, and stamp.

  9. Crooked or undersized print: trim each photograph precisely and align it squarely within the box.

  10. Portrait that differs from the applicant’s current appearance: use a fresh image that supports immediate identification.

What to Do If Your Indian PAN Card Photo Is Rejected

A photo-related deficiency usually identifies a practical correction: size, quantity, background, print clarity, attachment, or signature placement. Use the deficiency message as the checklist for a fresh submission.

  1. Identify the exact issue stated by the PAN service or processing authority.

  2. Prepare two fresh 35 × 45 mm colour prints on a white background.

  3. Attach the prints with adhesive and complete the left-photo signature and right-photo clarity check.

  4. Resubmit through the channel stated in the deficiency notice and keep the acknowledgement for tracking.

PhotoGov is an independent service. The Income Tax Department and its authorised PAN service channels make the final acceptance decision. This guide reflects the current official forms and government guidance available for 2026 applications.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Are the Official Indian PAN Card Photo Requirements?

An individual applicant submits two recent colour photos with plain white backgrounds, each in the 3.5 × 4.5 cm (35 × 45 mm) format. Sign or place a left-thumb impression across the left photo and the form. Keep the right photo clear, and fix both prints with photo adhesive.

What Is the Indian PAN Card Photo Size in Millimetres?

The current PAN card photo size is 35 × 45 mm (4.5 × 3.5 cm).

What Is the PAN Card Photo Size in Pixels?

At 300 DPI, the PAN size is 413 × 531 pixels. At 600 DPI — 826 × 1062 pixels. The official Forms 93 and 95 specify the physical 35 × 45 mm dimensions, while the pixel setting depends on the print resolution.

How Many Photos Are Required for a PAN Card Application?

Form No. 93 and Form No. 95 require two matching recent colour photographs for an individual applicant. Both photographs fit the 4.5 × 3.5 cm boxes printed on the form.

Does a PAN Card Photo Need a White Background?

Yes. The current Income Tax Department filing guidelines specify a white background. Use an evenly lit white surface with clear separation around the applicant’s head and shoulders.

Where Do I Sign the PAN Card Photographs?

Place the signature or left-thumb impression across the left photograph so one part appears on the image and the other part appears on the form. Preserve the right photograph as a clean portrait. Add the final signature or left-thumb impression inside the declaration box on the last page.

Can I Use a Left-Thumb Impression?

Yes. The form accepts a left-thumb impression. The impression requires attestation by a Magistrate, Notary Public, Oath Commissioner, or Gazetted Officer under official seal and stamp.

Are Glasses Allowed in a PAN Card Photo?

The current form uses facial clarity as the eyewear-related quality test. A glasses-free portrait delivers the clearest eye area. Clear everyday glasses also support a usable image when the lenses stay transparent and reflection-free.

How Recent Should a PAN Card Photo Be?

The official guideline uses the term “recent colour photographs” and sets the practical test as current identification. Use a newly captured portrait that closely matches the applicant’s appearance on the filing date.

Do Minors Need PAN Card Photos?

Yes. The current guidelines include minors in the two-photo rule. Prepare two recent colour photographs with white backgrounds in the 35 × 45 mm portrait format and complete the Representative Assessee section where applicable.

Does Instant e-PAN Require a Photo Upload?

Instant e-PAN uses Aadhaar e-KYC and completes identity verification through the Aadhaar record. The service skips a separate scanned photo and signature upload. Eligible applicants receive a valid e-PAN through the online process.

Can I Take a PAN Card Photo with a Smartphone?

Yes. Use another person to hold the smartphone at eye level, create soft front lighting, and stand against a smooth white background. Save the sharpest portrait, crop it to 35 × 45 mm, and print two matching copies at exact size.

How Is a PAN Card Photo Different from an Indian Passport Photo?

Both documents use a 35 × 45 mm portrait footprint in the current workflow. The PAN application requires two prints and a specific left-photo signature placement. The Indian passport process follows its own biometric framing and submission rules; review PhotoGov’s Indian passport photo guide for that separate standard.

Can I Use the Old 35 × 25 mm PAN Photo Size?

The 35 × 25 mm format belongs to the earlier Form 49A and Form 49AA workflow. Current individual applications use the 35 × 45 mm portrait boxes shown on Form No. 93 and Form No. 95.
